work_or_witness: Bari Gongju / Baridegi regional narrative songs · Definition; Munjeonbonpuri and Chasabonpuri · Definition
definition: A narrative song performed in Korean shamanic ritual; Bari Gongju is performed in rites for guiding the dead and Munjeonbonpuri explains Jeju household deities.
cultural_caution: A performed sacred/living genre, not a lore delivery mechanism or a spell category. The cited entries document different regional and Jeju contexts.

supports: Bari Gongju is a seosamuga sung in rites guiding the dead.
Munjeonbonpuri is a Jeju ritual seosamuga.

work_or_witness: Bari Gongju / Baridegi regional narrative songs · Regional characteristics
definition: The ritual-specialist category associated with Korean shamanic narrative performance and the broader organization of Bari Gongju variants.
cultural_caution: The English ‘shaman’ crosswalk is functional and imprecise; mudang is not a fantasy class and individual practitioners are not introduced as character nodes here.

supports: Bari Gongju’s transmission pattern is described in relation to types of mudang and shamanic music regions.

work_or_witness: Collected oral-folktale types: Fox-Marble Tale and Dokkaebi tales · Definition; Contents; Current status
definition: A label for variants of the Fox-Marble Tale, in which a fox may transform into a woman; the cited overview reports especially frequent transmission in northern regions.
cultural_caution: Do not treat gumiho as a fixed ‘female fox monster,’ a universal Korean creature species, or an automatic analogue to Chinese or Japanese fox traditions. The recorded tales have variants and specific social contexts.

supports: The tale is also called ‘Gumiho and Yeouiguseul’; its fox transforms into a woman in reported types, and regional transmission varies.

work_or_witness: Collected oral-folktale types: Fox-Marble Tale and Dokkaebi tales · Definition; Contents; Samguk Yusa, ‘Tohwa-nyeo and Bihyeong-rang’ account · Contents
definition: Transformation is directly attested in the selected fox-story witnesses: the fox in Fox-Marble Tale transforms into a woman, and Gil Dal turns into a fox in the Bihyeongrang account.
cultural_caution: This is only a witness-grounded narrative event; it does not posit an across-corpus transformation system or a universal gumiho rule.

supports: The Fox-Marble Tale describes a fox transformed into a woman.
Gil Dal turns into a fox.

work_or_witness: Korean Mythology and Folklore · Characteristics; Significance/Evaluation; Korean Mythology and Folklore · Legends; Characteristics
definition: A highly variable figure in Korean legends and folktales: accounts include visible and non-visible forms, interaction with people, abundance, mischief, and regional Jeju figures such as Yeonggam.
cultural_caution: Do not translate mechanically as ‘goblin,’ ‘demon,’ or ghost, and do not map it to the atlas’s Goblin-Faerie Beings solely by label. This pass includes no named dokkaebi character because the selected witnesses do not supply one.

supports: Dokkaebi depictions vary in form and narrative role and have a dual, changing status in lore.
Dokkaebi tales include regional legends and differing visible/non-visible forms.

work_or_witness: Collection highlight: ‘Mountain Spirit (Sansin) with Tiger Avatar’; Nationality/Period and Category
definition: Mountain Spirit is the collection title for a Joseon Buddhist painting showing Sansin with a tiger avatar.
cultural_caution: A museum object attests one Joseon Buddhist painting context only. Sansin is not a generic guardian-spirit species, a single universal character, or evidence that folk-religious and Buddhist layers are identical.

citations.locator: Collection highlight: ‘Mountain Spirit (Sansin) with Tiger Avatar’; Nationality/Period and Category
supports: The National Museum of Korea identifies a Joseon Buddhist painting as Mountain Spirit (Sansin) with Tiger Avatar.

work_or_witness: Munjeonbonpuri and Chasabonpuri · Definition; Contents, conclusion; Korean Mythology and Folklore · Contents
definition: In the Jeju Munjeonbonpuri account, Yeosan Buin is revived and installed as jowangsin; the narrative explains household deity relations.
cultural_caution: This does not make jowangsin a generic household-spirit race. Historical accounts also note Buddhist and Chinese associations, which remain separate contextual layers.

supports: Munjeonbonpuri explains household deity relations and installs Yeosan Buin as jowangsin.
The jowangsin entry distinguishes Korean evidence and notes Buddhist and Chinese associations as separate contexts.

work_or_witness: Bari Gongju / Baridegi regional narrative songs · Meaning; Korean Mythology and Folklore · Contents
definition: The realm of the dead in the selected Bari Gongju and Chasabonpuri accounts. Bari’s overview specifically describes a horizontally approached rather than vertically layered infernal space.
cultural_caution: Do not replace jeoseung with a standard fantasy hell/underworld map. Its spatial model, moral order, and ritual function vary by witness and genre.

supports: Bari Gongju reflects an otherworld/underworld conceived as horizontally reachable rather than vertically arranged.
Gangnim travels to the underworld and serves its death-messenger system.

work_or_witness: Korean Mythology and Folklore · Contents, opening explanation and Gangnim conclusion
definition: Underworld agent who receives a document and rope, verifies a person’s register, and takes those whose allotted life is finished; Gangnim is appointed to this role in Chasabonpuri.
cultural_caution: Psychopomp is only a functional comparison. Chasa belongs to a particular Jeju ritual narrative and its underworld administration, not a universal ‘reaper’ class.

citations.locator: Contents, opening explanation and Gangnim conclusion
supports: The entry explains chasa duties and narrates Gangnim’s appointment as a chasa.

work_or_witness: Bari Gongju / Baridegi regional narrative songs · Meaning
definition: An ethical concept explicitly discussed in the Bari Gongju overview, where Bari’s actions for her parents are interpreted through filial devotion.
cultural_caution: This is a Confucian ethical layer in an interpretation of a shamanic narrative, not proof that the narrative can be reduced to Confucian doctrine or to a game-mechanical obligation.

supports: The entry explicitly discusses filial devotion in Bari’s saving of her parents and contrasts kinship priorities.
